source_text: Καὶ οἱ μὲν περὶ τὰ εἴδωλα αὐτοὺς ἕλκοντες οἱ δαίμονές εἰσιν οἱ προειρημένοι, οἱ προστετηκότες τῷ ἀπὸ τῶν ἱερείων αἵματι καὶ ταῦτα περιλιχμώμενοι· οἱ δὲ τοῖς πολλοῖς ἀρέσκοντες θεοὶ καὶ ταῖς εἰκόσιν ἐπονομαζόμενοι, ὡς ἔστιν ἐκ τῆς κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς ἱστορίας εἰδέναι, ἄνθρωποι γεγόνασιν. Καὶ τους μὲν δαίμονας εἶναι τοὺς ἐπιβατεύοντας τοῖς ὀνόμασι πίστις ἡ ἑκάστου αὐτῶν ἐνέργεια. Οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἀποτέμνουσι τὰ αἰδοῖα, οἱ περὶ τὴν Ῥέαν, οἱ δὲ ἐγκόπτουσιν ἢ ἐντέμνουσιν, οἱ περὶ τὴν Ἄρτεμιν, καὶ ἡ μὲν ἐν Ταύροις φονεύει τοὺς ξένους· ἐῶ γὰρ τοὺς ταῖς μαχαίραις καὶ τοῖς ἀστραγάλοις αἰκιζομένους αὐτοὺς λέγειν καὶ ὅσα εἴδη δαιμόνων· οὐ γὰρ θεοῦ κινεῖν ἐπὶ τὰ παρὰ φύσιν. Ὅταν δ᾿ ὁ δαίμων ἀνδρὶ πορσύνῃ κακά, Τὸν νοῦν ἔβλαψε πρῶτον. Ὁ δὲ θεός, τελείως ἀγαθὸς ὤν, ἀϊδίως ἀγαθοποιός ἐστιν. Τοῦ τοίνυν ἄλλους μὲν εἶναι τοὺς ἐνεργοῦντας, ἐφ᾿ ἑτέρων δὲ ἀνίστασθαι τὰς εἰκόνας, ἐκεῖνο μέγιστον τεκμήριον, Τρωὰς καὶ Πάριον· ἡ μὲν Νερυλλίνου εἰκόνας ἔχει, ὃς ἀνὴρ τῶν καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς, τὸ δὲ Πάριον Ἀλεξάνδρου καὶ Πρωτέως· τοῦ Ἀλεξάνδρου ἔτι ἐπὶ τῆς ἀγορᾶς καὶ ὁ τάφος καὶ ἡ εἰκών.Οἱ μὲν οὖν ἄλλοι ἀνδριάντες τοῦ Νερυλλίνου κόσμημά εἰσι δημόσιον, εἴπερ καὶ τούτοις κοσμεῖται πόλις, εἷς δὲ αὐτῶν καὶ χρηματίζειν καὶ ἰᾶσθαι νοσοῦντας νομίζεται, καὶ θύουσί τε δι᾿ αὐτὰ καὶ χρυσῷ περιαλείφουσι καὶ στεφανοῦσι τὸν ἀνδριάντα οἱ Τρωαδεῖς. Ὁ δὲ τοῦ Ἀλεξάνδρου καὶ ὁ τοῦ Πρωτέως (τοῦτον δ᾿ οὐκ ἀγνοεῖτε ῥίψαντα ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸ πῦρ περὶ τὴν Ὀλυμπίαν), ὁ μὲν καὶ αὐτὸς λέγεται χρηματίζειν, τῷ δὲ τοῦ Ἀλεξάνδρου [Δύσπαρι, εἶδος ἄριστε, γυναιμανές] δημοτελεῖς ἄγονται θυσίαι καὶ ἑορταὶ ὡς ἐπηκόῳ θεῷ. Πότερον οὖν ὁ Νερυλλῖνος καὶ ὁ Πρωτεὺς καὶ ὁ Ἀλέξανδρός εἰσιν οἱ ταῦτα ἐνεργοῦντες περὶ τὰ ἀγάλματα ἢ τῆς ὕλης ἡ σύστασις; Ἀλλ᾿ ἡ μὲν ὕλη χαλκός ἐστιν. Τί δαὶ χαλκὸς δύναται καθ᾿ ἑαυτόν, ὃν μεταποιῆσαι πάλιν εἰς ἕτερον σχῆμα ἔξεστιν, ὡς τὸν ποδονιπτῆρα ὁ παρὰ τῷ Ἡροδότῳ Ἄμασις; Ὁ δὲ Νερυλλῖνος καὶ ὁ Πρωτεὺς καὶ ὁ Ἀλέξανδρος τί πλέον τοῖς νοσοῦσιν; Ἃ γὰρ ἡ εἰκὼν λέγεται νῦν ἐνεργεῖν, ἐνήργει καὶ ζῶντος καὶ νοσοῦντος Νερυλλίνου.
pass_a_gloss: And the demons, the ones previously mentioned, who have been drawn to the idols, they are the ones who have been assigned to the blood from the sacrifices and these things are licked by them; and the ones pleasing to the many and named gods and images, as it is to know from the history concerning them, have become men. And faith, the activity of each of them, is what the demons are, the ones going upon the names. For some cut off their genitals, the ones concerning Rhea, and some castrate or cut out, the ones concerning Artemis, and the one in Tauris kills the strangers; for I permit the ones being mistreated by the swords and the dice to speak and the kinds of demons; for it is not the nature of God to move towards the things contrary to nature. When the demon brings evils to a man, he first harms the mind. But God, being completely good, is always doing good. Therefore, the fact that others are the ones acting and the images are being set up on others, this is the greatest proof, Troy and Paris; the one has images of Neryllinus, who is a man among us, and the other has images of Alexander and Proteus; and the tomb and the image of Alexander are still in the marketplace. The other statues of Neryllinus are a public ornament, if indeed the city is also ornamented by these things, and one of them is even thought to prophesy and heal the sick, and the Trojans sacrifice through them and anoint with gold and crown the statue. And the one of Alexander and the one of Proteus (and you are not unaware that he threw himself into the fire concerning Olympia), the one is also said to prophesy, and public sacrifices and festivals are led to the one of Alexander as to a listening god. Which ones then, Neryllinus and Proteus and Alexander, are the ones acting concerning these statues, or is it the composition of the material? But the material is bronze. What then can bronze do by itself, which it is possible to reshape again into another form, like the foot-basin which Amasis, the one by Herodotus, made? And what more do Neryllinus and Proteus and Alexander do for the sick? For whatever the image is said to be doing now, it was also doing when Neryllinus was alive and sick.

choices.why: applied to the sacrifices and festivals led to Alexander

pass_b_english: The demons I mentioned earlier are the ones drawn to the idols, assigned to the blood from sacrifices, and licking it up. The figures popularly called gods and honored with images, as their own histories show, were actually human beings. It is the power of each person's belief that makes demons the ones who act on those names. Some castrate themselves, the devotees of Rhea; others mutilate or cut themselves, the devotees of Artemis; and the one in Tauris murders strangers. I will let those abused by swords and dice describe their sufferings and the kinds of demons involved, for it is not in God's nature to drive anyone toward what is contrary to nature. When a demon brings evils upon a man, it first damages his mind. But God, being perfectly good, is eternally doing good.

Therefore, the fact that the ones acting are different from the ones on whom the images are modeled is the strongest proof. Take Troy and Parium: Troy has images of Neryllinus, a man of our own time, while Parium has images of Alexander and Proteus; Alexander's tomb and image still stand in the marketplace. The other statues of Neryllinus serve as public ornaments, if a city can be adorned by such things, and one of them is even thought to prophesy and heal the sick. The Trojans sacrifice through them, anoint the statue with gold, and crown it. Alexander's statue and Proteus's statue (you know he threw himself into the fire at Olympia) are likewise said to prophesy, and public sacrifices and festivals are led to Alexander's as to a listening god. So then, are Neryllinus, Proteus, and Alexander the ones acting through these statues, or is it the composition of the material? But the material is bronze. What can bronze do by itself, when it can be melted down and reshaped into another form, like the foot-basin Amasis made, the one Herodotus mentions? And what more can Neryllinus, Proteus, and Alexander do for the sick? For whatever the image is said to do now, it was doing back when Neryllinus was alive and sick.

review.notes: Pass A fails to translate the clause 'ἐκεῖνο μέγιστον τεκμήριον, Τρωὰς καὶ Πάριον' correctly, rendering it as 'this is the greatest proof, Troy and Paris', whereas the Greek refers to the cities/regions Troy and Parium (the text uses 'Πάριον' as a noun/place name, which Pass B correctly identifies as 'Parium'). More critically, Pass A fails on the clause 'ἐῶ γὰρ τοὺς ταῖς μαχαίραις καὶ τοῖς ἀστραγάλοις αἰκιζομένους αὐτοὺς λέγειν καὶ ὅσα εἴδη δαιμόνων', translating it as 'for I permit the ones being mistreated by the swords and the dice to speak and the kinds of demons', which is a nonsensical rendering of the Greek. The Greek 'ἐῶ... λέγειν' (I allow/let... to speak) refers to the speaker allowing the victims to speak of their sufferings/the demons, but Pass A's syntax 'permit the ones... to speak and the kinds of demons' is broken. Furthermore, Pass A's translation of 'ἐπηκόῳ θεῷ' as 'listening god' is a literalist error for 'attendant/accompanying god' (though Pass B's 'listening' is also questionable, Pass A's failure on the 'speak' clause is a primary semantic failure).
reasons: Pass A fails to render the sense of 'ἐῶ γὰρ τοὺς ταῖς μαχαίραις καὶ τοῖς ἀστραγάλοις αἰκιζομένους αὐτοὺς λέγειν καὶ ὅσα εἴδη δαιμόνων' (for I allow the ones being mistreated by swords and dice to speak [of] the kinds of demons), resulting in a broken English sentence: 'for I permit the ones being mistreated by the swords and the dice to speak and the kinds of demons'.
